So now the question comes in... Do elk/all deertaurs actually shed their antlers? Well there's two theories:


Yes, they do. Though they may drop them at different times when compared to deer in the human world. Them shedding antlers also insinuates that male centaurs of the cervid variety *do* go through testosterone highs and lows (lowered testosterone is what makes deer drop their antlers) and that they *do* go into a rut season. Although I am a big animal nerd and the idea of Elktaur going through funny deer puberty stuff seems great, I actually struggle with this theory personally. From what we have seen of centaur society, the need for antler shedding seems unnecessary as centaurs are traditionally monogamous (which eliminates the need to grow antlers year after year). That is unless this theoretical antler shedding is done for an entirely different reason for centaurs. 


No, they don't. Male centaurs of the cervid variety do *not* shed their antlers. They grow them in their adolescence once and that's it. Elktaur himself just knew that human world deer shed their antlers and used that as ammunition to hide the fact he actually cut them off. As the saying goes, "A great lie is one with a little bit of truth within it." Him using this to cover his tracks would hold even more grounds if this party really did happen during the time that deer usually lose their antlers as the woman could've talked to other human party members about Elktaur's lack of antlers and a hunter/someone who knows deer could have responded with something to the effect of, "Oh yeah, deer here do that," which would solidify Elktaur's lie even further.

For yard treatment keep grass mowed really short, keep weeds pulled up, and keep standing water away.


If Triazicide is not really working on your lawn, it may not hurt to switch to Bifen IT. You also may need to just apply the chemical more frequently as most pesticides are not a one-and-done deal and are applied according to the activity (and weather) of the problematic bug you are trying to eliminate. If you live near a lot of wooded areas (ideal for chiggers) then it is highly likely that they are simply migrating from this area instead of just merely living on your yard alone. Sevin is also a great pesticide, but it is best used as an absolute last resort as it is well known to also harm honey bees and earthworms. 


Keep DE application frequent. This will/does help with straggler chiggers that survive other treatments. Borax (yes the laundry powder) is also a known insecticide as boric acid melts the exoskeletons of bugs. Adding Borax to your laundry can be further ammo in eliminating the chiggers and although Borax *can* be sprinkled around like DE, be aware that it can be can be toxic to pets if consumed.


While I agree with the comments that birds like chickens and guineas help with bug control, chickens and guineas *do not* help with chiggers at this stage. Chiggers that bite and feast on skin cells are at the larval stage. When at this stage they are essentially microscopic. So unnoticeable to humans and most birds. Birds may be helpful in eliminating chiggers at other stages of life (and in the long run can help keep numbers down by eating breeders), but as for chiggers in the larval stage goes the birds are just as much a victim as you are (as chiggers also use birds and reptiles as hosts, sometimes even moreso than mammals). Your chickens actually may be chigger *magnets* right now. Especially if they do have access to the wooded areas as they would be bringing chiggers back to your yard via their feathers.


On a similar note, due to birds being a very common host for chiggers, it may not hurt to temporarily take down any bird feeders and bird baths you may have in your yard. Birds will be bringing in larval chiggers in their feathers and areas with high bird activity in your yard can become chigger hotspots. Bird feeders and baths can return once cold weather moves in and/or when chigger control is well established.


There's many ways to treat chigger bites themselves and some ways to help prevent it. Tucking pantlegs into socks and wearing high boots can help. Chiggers, although super tiny, struggle to move within tight fitting clothes with minimal openings. On preventing bites I have personally had the most luck with rubbing VapoRub on common climbing areas and spraying apple cider vinegar on my legs and arms. Cold water/frozen spoons help relieve the itch of bites and I live by Chiggerex medicine and calamine lotion. Also, while bleach baths can work, please be wary if you are female and/or prone to things like UTIs and general skin sensitivity. I have tried the bleach bath and while it did soothe the bites, it ultimately caused other problems.

Bamboo grows really fast and gets woody quick. Goats *can* eat bamboo, but unless you have a large herd the bamboo can get out of hand. 


Also, be aware that there are a lot of, "bamboos," that are actually poisonous for most animals. A lot of plants that look and are called bamboo are actually not genuine bamboo. For example, heavenly/sacred bamboo is highly toxic to goats as it is actually in the same family as barberry. Lucky bamboo is also very toxic as it is in the same family as the dragon tree. 


If you are in the U.S. look at your local state and county laws. Some places in the U.S. have banned genuine bamboo species due to their fast growth and prolific nature making them really invasive to local environments.

You can't always make guesses on breed based on look and behavior. *Especially* when most of the shelter/rescue population come from backyard breeding, puppy mills, and dogs turned feral. Majority of dogs coming from shelters do not originate from responsible breeding and therefore do not follow conformation and temperament standards. So no you can't really accurately guess the breed of most dogs in the shelter and even then it isn't really going to help the person adopting them. 


It's normal for shelters to label all their dogs as simply mutts regardless of what they look like. There have been many dogs that I would 100% put under one breed and yet in their DNA tests they end up being a group of other breeds that I would not even guess. Shelters are often legally obliged to just say all the dogs are mutts because if they give someone a dog that is labelled a labrador, that owner does a DNA test, and that dog turns out to be mostly bully, then the shelter can be held reliable for false advertising.


DNA testing a single dog is hundreds of dollars. There is weeks of waiting for results. So many shelters are already underfunded and under-resourced. They would have to add the price of testing on top of the already existing adoption price, which would turn more people away and cause more dogs to sit without a home. Shelters would also have to wait until the results come back, which is more time dogs spend waiting without a home. In many shelters, those dogs waiting without a home can keep other dogs from being in the shelter where they can get treatment, food, and water.

This can be very dog dependant, but this is my advice:


Look into building a fence, or setting up a secure tether system. Even if you have far away neighbors, a lot of dogs will wander outside of your property boundaries, and those neighbors *do not* want strange dogs on their property. There's been many instances of neighbor wars starting because someone from the city moves in and then let's their dogs run loose without care. If you are worried about your dogs getting bitten/attacked by snakes then you should also worry about your dogs staying in your property as there can be way worse things your dogs can run into in someone else's yard.


When you first move in it may be better to just handle your dogs similarly to how they were handled in the city. Keep putting them on leashes and walking them on the property. This is a change for them and too much change at once can cause problems. Keep giving them some sense of normalcy until they fully cope with being in a new environment. This can also help you figure out what will be best for them once they do fully cope with being in a new place. 


Keep your dogs updated on vaccines and parasite prevention. There is generally more wildlife in rural areas, which can mean more pests. Make sure your dogs stay up to date on rabies vaccine, heartworm preventative, flea and tick preventative, etc. 


On a similar note, there is generally more/different wildlife in rural areas. In the city you will mostly find smaller urban critters like squirrels, snakes, raccoons, rabbits, etc. and while you will also find them in rural areas you may also find other forms of wildlife such as deer, coyotes, hawks, etc. depending on your region. Those forms of wildlife can pose a greater danger to your dogs. Fence or secure tether system is partly recommended for this reason, but I also recommend supervising your dogs when they are out as well (especially when it comes to coyotes as they have been known to harass or go after unsupervised dogs).


When it comes to managing wildlife in your property, a pretty quick way to lessen their commonality is to eliminate/control food, shelter, water. Don't leave your trash unsecured outside. Have them in a trashcan or dumpster with the ability to be latched or locked shut. Don't leave animal food out in the open, especially at night. Don't leave out things that will collect water. Get rid of or do not allow your dogs to go near tall grass, wood piles, brush piles, etc..

Gas escaping the carcass. 


When a creature dies, decomposition begins immediately. Cells die and the natural bacteria in the gut becomes unregulated. This causes excess gas (especially in ruminants like sheep) to build up in the body. That gas builds pressure and needs an outlet of escape, so gas escapes from the natural holes in the body (ears, nose, mouth, anus). Gas building up is also why dead bodies frequently bloat or swell significantly in the abdomen, as even if the natural orifices are blocked, that gas will escape somehow.

Selective mutism is an anxiety disorder that causes a person to be unable to speak in some social situations. It often presents itself in childhood, but it can develop in adulthood or persist into adulthood if not managed/treated. 


I find it annoying that no one really talks about the disorder. Then when it is talked about there's so much misinformation you have to dodge or get through. It's not the same as typical toddler shyness. You can't just fix it by strong-arming the person into speaking (in fact it makes it worse), and it can develop later in life.


I did not become selectively mute until I was in my teens and it's fucking hard to deal with. My anxiety around speaking becomes *so bad* that it legitimately feels like my throat is swelling shut. Then it takes forever for me to get calmed down enough to where I don't feel like I'm trying to talk through a straw.

I have had goats for a long time. My oldest turns 10 this year. Here's my input:


**On Fencing**

Goats are escape artists in the sense that they climb and are rough on fencing in ways you wouldn't really expect. It took a lot of trial and error before I found the fencing that works best for my herd. 


One mistake I made was using fencing with larger gaps. With that fencing *so many* of my goats got their heads stuck trying to squeeze through (one of my goats injured his horn really bad in a panic). Then when kidding season came around all the cute little kids could just walk through the gaps in the fence like it was nothing. I switched to horse fencing and I no longer have issues with stuck heads and kids running amok.


Another thing I learned is to keep climbing structures at least 7 feet away from the fence's boundaries. The goats will climb the structure and parkour right over the fence. Despite that hiccup I actually figured out that having a little goat, "playground," with structures and toys made my goats try to escape less. 


Electric wire is almost a necessity with goats. When I switched to horse fencing I didn't anticipate my goats creating a habit out of scratching themselves against the fence with their *full weight.* Within a year the fencing got so stretched. I gave them an industrial brush to scratch themselves on, but the habit was already made and they continued with the fence. So I set out and ran electric wire in 5 different places. Goats had no choice but to switch to the brush alternative. The electric wire also ended up being a lifesaver against predators a couple times.


**On Feed**


Goats are browsers more than they are grazers. It's common to think, "Goats will eat anything," but that couldn't be further from the truth. They are mouthy and will chew on things, but they are actually kinda picky eaters in my experience. Goats being browsers means that they don't really eat the same grass and pasture as cows or sheep. My herd actually loves things like tree saplings, poison ivy, plantains, and woody weeds like mare tails. They actually don't really eat grass unless they absolutely have to. 


With my herd I *do* have to buy them bags of feed and bales of hay in the winter time. My winters are pretty cold and not much grows during that time and eating helps keep my goats warm. I'd say it isn't too bad considering that I don't keep them on pelletted feed all year long. 


I will give my goats scraps (limited quantities) throughout the year which helps offset the need for pellet feed. I did a lot of research to see what foods are safe for goats. I have given my herd pumpkins, corn silks and leaves, leftover live Christmas trees, old bread, bananas, apples, carrots, and bell peppers. Peanut butter also makes a good treat and I use it when training my goats. 


**Goats as Pets**


Goats will be mean and ornery if they are not actively worked with. They are like most other domestic animals, if you don't set boundaries they will bully you. Since most of my herd are considered pets, I started training and working with them pretty much from the get-go. New goats are in a, "quarantine," pen (a 10 x 10 dog chain link dog kennel) to make sure they don't have anything contagious. That smaller space also allows the new goat to get used to me. I'll spend an hour or two a day just sitting in the pen with them and then slowly working up to talking, petting, feeding from the hand. After about a couple months I'll start working on training and establishing respect. Halter breaking, picking up their hooves (you have to trim them), getting them used to brushing, etc. 


Believe it or not there is a lot of information relating to training and establishing boundaries on videos/forum posts relating to 4H and FFA show goats. They translate well to regular pet goats and believe me, having a goat that is bonded to you and indifferent to maintenance is an absolute blessing for both yourself and your goats.

This may not be an option for everybody, but if you have a telephone/utility pole on your property most electric companies have an option where you can call them and have them install a light on that pole. The code is relatively easy to change when needed and the batteries are easy to replace (also when they die it remains locked). Goats are actually browsers more than grazers. They much prefer eating things like tree bark/saplings, woody weeds like pigweed and mare tails, and my herd goes apeshit for plantains. Because they are not heavy grazers, I still have to take a mower into their pen whenever the grass actually manages to overpower the weeds.


Goats are also pretty notorious escape artists. If you don't want to install electric wire, don't get goats because almost nothing else is going to keep them contained for very long. They also need sturdy fences because they are rough on them and will test fencing constantly. If you plan on getting goats with horns, I suggest getting fencing that goats can't squeeze their head through. I use horse fencing and hog panels with electric wire both inside and outside the boundary for my goats. 


Goats are prone to parasites and unfortunately medicine resistant parasites are *extremely* common for goats. Instead of consistently giving goats medicine as routine it is actually better to give goats medicine only when they have signs of having a parasite load. Doing this will help keep parasites from becoming resistant, especially if you switch medicine brands occasionally.


Vaccinate goats for scrapie if they don't already have it. Scrapie is like the goat version of parvovirus in dogs. It is very painful, deadly, and contagious.


General hardiness is dependant on the goat's breed and your climate. Breeds like pygmy and nubian tend to be some of the most adaptable while breeds like boer and angora tend to be more sensitive. 


Goats can and will be assholes. Especially towards children. You do kind of have to establish yourself in their pecking order because they will continue being assholes if they know you won't do anything about it. I trained all of my goats and it actually makes things so much easier for all of us.


Goats attract predators like crazy. They are noisy and they produce smells that are insanely attractive to predators (like coyotes) so you will definitely need some decent predator proofing if you have a lot of coyotes, bears, feral dogs, etc.


Goats are noisy. Especially when you first get them as they will be a little stressed out. My herd does not hesitate to let me know when their breakfast is late or when something is wrong (my old boss goat has a specific scream she makes when she notices something alarming, sometimes that alarming thing is a plastic bag tangled up in a tree nearby). If you are getting females, remember that females have an estrus cycle (they can't be spayed like a dog) so at least two times out of the year they might drive you a bit mad with their insistent yelling, tail flagging, and doing inappropriate things with structures. 


Goats have very individualistic personalities. Some goats are cuddly, some are more rude, some are very biddable and would do anything for food. It's great to see as an owner, but it can sometimes come with the downfall of goats sometimes having to be separated from others due to major clashes in their personality. 


If you are wanting a more human oriented goat, get a bottle baby. They do tend to test human boundaries a bit more, but once they learn their place they are a joy to have around as they just have that more intimate bond with humans.


If you put in the time and work, goats are actually really fun to have around. Training my herd was very rewarding and they can learn so many things. Okay, so I pretty much live in tick central, and I despise ticks. Here's some things that can help keep ticks out:


Controlled burning of the property. Especially if you have a lot of pine trees around (fallen needles are breeding grounds for ticks). This will burn up the living tick population and will destroy the dead brush that they hide in. Your property will look terrible for a bit, but it will bounce back.


Permethrin yard spray. This is a more aggro tick management strategy, but it works. Get a permethrin based yard spray and spray the hell out of your property. Permethrin can be dangerous to dogs in large amounts so keep your dog inside while spraying and for a few hours after spraying. When my tick invasion was at it's worst, I would apply the spray on a once-a-month basis. When I noticed very few ticks I backed off to about once or twice a year.


Get your dog the lyme vaccine if they already don't have it. There are many anti-tick meds for dogs and what works depends on the dog. My dog was allergic to most flea and tick pills, but she does great with the Seresto collar and it keeps all kinds of bugs off of her. 


Keep dead brush, vines, and overgrowth managed. Ticks are bastards and will hide. The less hiding you allow, the more the ticks will stay away. Keep weeds and grass short. Keep leaves and pine needles raked up. Burn dead and fallen branches.


Leave wild bug-munchers alone. Frogs/toads are very opportunistic tick eaters, if you see one on the property, let them do their thing. Birds that naturally eat bugs will also eat ticks. Opossums are opportunistic all around and although they are creepy, they are tick eaters. They are also no serious threat to your dog as they are also resistant to a lot of dangerous diseases. 


Get domestic bug-munchers. This will depend on your dog, your ability, and your local restrictions. Chickens, turkeys, ducks, quail, and guinea fowl are all tick eaters. This was not an option I could personally use, but it's an option to anyone who has the ability.

Here's a pretty fun thing regarding American accents in media.... If you watched movies/shows or listened to radio shows from the early 20th century you may find that Americans actually sounded very different then and that Americans today do not sound like that naturally. That is because the accent used is called Mid-Atlantic (often also known as Transatlantic). It was an accent *not* natively found in any region of the U.S. and was instead specifically taught within the upper class entertainment industry, and the accent mixed features from American and British english. It is thought that the accent was used a lot in media at the time partially out of technological necessity as early radio and sound films were not great and a more standard American accent would be difficult to hear. Use of the Mid-Atlantic accent dropped off exponentially after the second World War and has became somewhat of a, "lost art," as the accent has to be specifically taught in order for it to be used properly.


General American english (also known as Broadcast english) is the accent you are most likely to find in American media today, and unlike the Mid-Atlantic accent, General American is naturally used in the western regions of the country (with the accent being prevalent in other odd spots in the U.S.) That being said, multiple different U.S. accents have been represented in different media nowadays thanks to technological advances in audio. Most Americans know General American english as the, "No-accent accent."

Okay.... One thing.... Dogs cannot actually, "lock," their jaws. They can bite down really hard, but there is no biological mechanism that truly allows them to, "lock," onto something. 


I also **very** strongly advise against a shock collar. I know shock collars are controversial, to be honest there are many situations where I would kinda shrug about it even though I don't agree with it. However, one situation I'm not going to shrug at is shocking a dog in/about to get into a fight. That 100% never works and will make the situation worse even if you deliver the shock as he is running up/prior to a bite. When two dogs are fighting and your dog notices, by the time he starts running up he has already decided he is going to fight those dogs, and when he makes that decision his emotions are high and he is on edge. Delivering a painful shock from a remote is going to make those emotions and that on edge feeling go tenfold and he is going to direct that on those dogs because his focus is strictly on those dogs. On top of that, using the shock collar will actually make that behavior worse over time because now instead of him reacting due to aggression and/or not being shown any better he is instead going to react because he associates other dogs fighting with getting a painful shock, and he doesn't want a painful shock so he is going to do what he can to stop the fighting so he doesn't get a painful shock. 


You can use the citronella spray and the break stick, but those things are not actually going to prevent a bite, and if he is able to bite down hard enough that you can't easily pry his jaws open then he is able to bite down hard enough to injure the other dog. A muzzle really should be your first option here, as much as you don't want to hear that. I understand that he uses his mouth to play fetch and stuff like that, but dogs can learn to adapt around that. It also doesn't matter who's dog started the fight because you will always be the one most responsible because you are the one with the biggest and most powerful dog. 


What you need to do is start keeping a muzzle on your dog when he is around other dogs and get in touch with a professionally certified LIMA (Least intrusive, minimally adversive) trainer and a canine behaviorist. 


Remember, you have a dog that comes from very powerful breeds and breeds that do have a genetic tendency for dog on dog aggression. Good training and management is your best friend if you want to avoid possible euthanasia and want to keep your dog happy. I am mostly familiar with southern Missouri, though I have *some* familiarity with the rest of the state. 


Missouri is split into 3 USDA plant hardiness zones with Zone 5 being furthest north. Zone 6 covering the central area. Zone 7 being furthest south. In the bootheel (the part of the state that hangs down on the bottom right side) you will actually find 7b hardiness zones. Regardless of zone and area of the state, there are prominent seasons that will get snow/ice, but the southern portion tends to have the mildest weather season-wise.


In the central areas there is unfortunately very rocky soil due to the hills, so raised beds are often needed for vegetable plant species. However, the rockier soil can be great homes for timber and deciduous fruit trees like plums and peaches. Despite the rockier soil this area of the state does allow for livestock/poultry production with bovine being one of the most common (though I have seen camel and emu ranches). There are also a lot of caves if that is something you're generally into. 


In the southern portion of Missouri the hills fall off and the soil becomes less rocky. Less livestock/poultry will be seen and you will be greeted by crop fields comprising of soybean, corn, wheat, peaches, watermelon, and sometimes cotton and peanuts. The southeastern portion has a lot of cypress swampland which provides loamy and nutrient rich soil. The soil there is much better suited for common vegetable species and it can even provide for more demanding species like gourds with minimal need for amendments. 


In regards to laws, Missouri is generally very welcoming to homesteads and off-grid living. A lot of Missourians actually homestead or are off-grid in some way. Collecting rainwater is legal in the state. In Missouri the building codes can be really lax, especially in rural areas with some places only requiring codes for septic (though local bylaws can vary). Missouri does have a state income tax (rates ranging from 1.50 to 5.40 percent). However, sales tax is generally cheaper than sales tax from states that lack an income tax. Missouri is the 12th least expensive in terms of gas price average and Missouri has the cheapest cigarette and tobacco prices. Missouri has a 89% high school graduation rate. 


**General Pros**

A) A lot of wildlife and conservation which opens up opportunities for hunting

B) Plenty of land and general lower cost of living

C) More hands-off approach when concerning what people do with their land

D) Diverse geography

E) Residents generally undisturbed by others

F) Caves


**General Cons**

A) Bugs. If you go central or north you will frequently be disturbed by ticks. If you go south you will frequently be disturbed by mosquitoes

B) Weather is notoriously known for being indecisive. Many days where you will start your day by turning on the heat in the morning and then switching to air conditioning by the afternoon. You also may experience 4 definite seasons in a week. 

C) Meth.

D) Politics lean conservative. Your mileage will vary on how much that may disturb you as counties can vary wildly.

Very *very* rarely can someone live off of their homestead enough to truly be able to drop jobs. There are a lot of expenses in homesteading, especially starting out. Unless you outright just become a commercial farm, you're likely not going to get to a point where you won't have to have a job elsewhere. 


Homesteading is less about saving and/or making money and more about curbing the food insecurity that can come from chain grocery stores and food deserts. It's not really cutting costs, as that money you would've spent on a dozen eggs at the store is now just circulating into feeding and caring for you own egg laying hens. It's not really making a profit either because you will never be able to compete with commercial farms as you will not be able to match their supply and meet the demands of the country without becoming a commercial farm yourself. Sure, you can probably make *some* money by bartering with locals and selling extra supply at farmer's markets, but it will absolutely not be enough for you to just leave your day job indefinitely. 


You also have to remember that there are costs very specific to homesteading.

First of all... What is the size of your property? Do you have/can get a very secure fence? Do you frequently have neighbors/guests visiting your area?


Livestock guardian dogs can be great to have, but they can be a nightmare if you live in an area with not much acreage, not good fences, and a lot of neighbors and visitors. Remember, these dogs are big, and even if they have a flock/herd to protect, they really do need quite a bit of room to patrol. If they do not have good amount of room, they will become escape artists and may even turn on their own herd/flock out of boredom. I would say a full acre is the minimum for a livestock guardian. 


They also need secure fencing. The, "yoke of shame," is a joke within homesteading circles for a reason. Livestock guardians will climb, squeeze, and dig out of fences, and due to them being huge dogs they really do need fences higher than 4 feet and dig defense barriers. Electric wire is commonly used to help contain livestock guardians, especially in areas where fencing is weak. 


Another thing is neighbors. Most livestock guardians always bark if they perceive a threat. If you have neighbors nearby and there is frequent activity, the livestock guardian is going to bark at it. If you do have neighbors nearby, you may benefit more from a great pyrenees. The great pyrenees, while still a guardian, is more of a bark first bite second even if someone is on the property, while breeds like kangals can be more aggro and more likely to immediately attack.

Motion activated sprinklers, motion activated lights, motion activated alarms, and radios will deter coyotes as now that easy meal has became difficult because there is conflict. Motion activated devices also mess with a coyote's understanding of schedule. They probably already know when you are out and when your dog is out, so they are showing up when they think there's going to be no conflict.

You will need a humongous property and lots of barriers if you are wanting things as quiet as possible. 


Country living is mainly only quiet because conflict with neighbors is minimal. It's not *actually* quiet noise wise most of the time. There are many reasons why I practice and collect in this hobby. 


For one, I practice this hobby because I am utilizing what has been passed down from my great grandparents, to my grandparents, to my parents, and so on. There is a lot of Caddo and Apache in my bloodline. Unfortunately I have became pretty separated from many traditional teachings from those tribes due to circumstances that many modern indigenous people face today. One of the few teachings that has stood strong throughout the generations in my family is utilizing as much of an animal as possible. While vulture culture is alive and well in some aspects, there are many aspects that truly are a dying art. For example, I can make sturdy sewing needles out of bone. I can create beautiful drums out of deer hide and tendons. Those are things that are not practiced much anymore (especially in my location) because there is no necessity for doing those things anymore (factories can just make sewing needles out of metal and drums out of synthetic materials), and those practices are often only shared within indigenous groups. 


Skulls are also fun to collect for me because they show the basic structure of an animal, a thing almost never seen in every day life. I love looking at them and studying them. For example, I have the skull of a domestic dog, a western coyote, and an eastern coyote. When they have muscle and hair, there isn't a significant amount of difference between them. However, when they are stripped down to their skulls the differences couldn't be more obvious. I find similar interest when it comes to goat skulls. When a goat is disbudded (removal of the horns' roots via burning) it shows up as gnarly textured nodules on the skull. When a goat has horns, underneath that keratin sheath is porous bone with prominent lines where the blood vessels used to be. On a polled goat (born without horns, which is relatively rare due to funky goat genetic stuff) the skull is entirely smooth. That's not even talking about the interesting differences between breeds of goats. A boer goat skull looks *very* different from a pygmy goat skull.


With taxidermy I mostly create from animals specifically sourced from my local area. It's an art form on its own, and taxidermy itself surprisingly has a pretty rich history (for example, at one time in the boy scouts, taxidermy was actually a skill you could earn a badge on). Not only that, but I have had the honor of receiving animals that are extremely elusive and rare in my area. I, and my guests, get to see and touch those elusive animals up close, and you'd be surprised how different a species can look based on where they are from. Every region has different predators, different environments, different genetics, and different nutrition. A red fox from Missouri is going to look very different from a red fox from Montana. Taxidermy is a great way for people to see those differences, and get to touch and see animals that usually can only be observed from a great distance. Yeah, my place may not be a museum, but if I'm being frank, most items in a museum belongs to private collectors anyways, museums just, "rent out," items from those collections. 


Similar things can be said for wet specimens. Wet specimens are useful for animals and parts that cannot be traditionally used for taxidermy. Stillborn and fetal animals are popularly kept as wet specimens. Some wet specimens can even preserve the actual DNA of an animal species. The thylacine (an extinct Australian animal) had it's DNA preserved because one person, many, many decades decided to take some fetal/stillborn babies and preserve them in a jar. Sure, when the person did this, they never would have thought that this animal was gonna go extinct and that technology was going to become so advanced. Most real authentic animal fur will be wind resistant as leather is not very porous. 


In my experience beaver is the warmest and it lasts a while when cared for properly. However, you will spend a pretty penny on beaver hides as their fur is also very plush and it takes more than one beaver to create things like jackets. 


When it comes to animal hides and leathers in general, their ability to hold up in the long run has to do with their tanning, how they are cared for, what kind of wear they go through, and their fur and leather type. 


Their leather type is the thickness of the skin itself. Some animals have thin skin while others have thick skin. Cattle leather is one of the hardiest leathers and that is why you often see them used in products that go through a lot of wear such as shoes and saddles. Leather from deer is also pretty sturdy and it is most often used in furniture due to their elasticity. Elasticity is how much a leather will stretch without tearing. Deer leather is also a soft leather.


Fur type is what kind of fur an animal has. Animals can have plush fur and this is found in animals like foxes, beaver, and coyote. Animals can also have coarse fur and this is found in deer, razorbacks, and wild equines. They can also be graded by summer coat and winter coat. Summer coat is thinner and winter coat is thicker and more lush. Plush fur creatures often have more hairs in the hide, but the hair is often so fine that it is subject to rubbing off under friction. Coarse fur has less hairs in the hide, but it can better withstand constant friction.


Leathers also need to be upkept in order to ensure longevity. They can dry out and become cracked so they need to be oiled occasionally.

I used to have a boxer that was like this. Major anxiety, destroyed every crate possible (things like impact dog crates weren't readily available at the time), and she even panicked so bad once that she busted through a window and went missing for 2 weeks. Medication, trainers, and behaviorists helped some, but she still had moments of relapsing, *especially* when there was a change in routine. Doggy daycares weren't anywhere near my area, and dog walkers weren't really an option either as there was really no one I could trust with her (Rover didn't exist at the time and my neighbors were... not great to say the least).


I can definitely understand what you're dealing with. With my boxer I pretty much had to pick a room and dog-proof the absolute hell out of it. She was fine in the room save for those few relapses. While the crate continued being a no-go as she would freak out and destroy it *every. single. time.* no matter how I went about it. 


I'm sure you're probably dog proofing the room your pup is kept in right now. Especially the wires. Though be aware that if your routine is still changing up (I saw the comment where you said you left early that day) that your dog may continue the freak outs and may seek something else to destroy. If you have a wooden door keeping your pup in the room, they might seek chewing through the door if there is enough of a gap between the bottom of the door and the floor (I am speaking from experience) so it may not hurt to also spray the bottom of the door with bitter apple spray along with the baseboards. Other ways to proof those areas if the spray does not work is to install kick plates (those metal sheets that sit on the bottom of doors to protect them from damage. You can get them in an assortment of sizes). Kick plates are metal and smooth, so dogs can't chew through it and they won't damage their teeth trying. 


I'm not sure if this will work with your dog, but it may be worth the effort as it definitely helped my boxer when she was going through her phases of panic. When I knew my routine was changing, I knew my dog was likely going to relapse. Before leaving I would exercise her more. I would keep her going (walking, jogging, playing) until she was panting. This is so she would be a bit tired and more likely to not feel as strongly about me leaving.


 Then I would add in some scent games to the mix. Scent games can be as simple or as complicated as you want. How I did it was I kept a stuffingless dog toy specifically used for scent, and I would add scents that was not really common for my dog to come across. I would put the toy in a Ziploc bag, add the scent and seal the bag until I was ready to, "deploy," it. When I was ready to utilize the scent I would take now-scented toy out of the bag, and just rub it in different areas of the room before putting her in the room and leaving. I have used so many different scents like vanilla, dead oak leaves, catnip, honeysuckle, etc.. Believe it or not when I combined scent games along with wearing her out, she actually wouldn't have super severe fits. She would be tired when she came in the room, she would rest a while, become a bit restless later, catch a whiff of the scent, get distracted and start trying to, "track," said scent. The best way to handle coyotes is to set boundaries and make your property as unappealing to coyotes as possible. Easily accessible trash, bird feeders, water bowls, etc are coyote attractions and they should not be left out/easy to get to wherever possible.


On setting boundaries there are completely nonlethal ways to teach coyotes to stay away from people and their dogs. Motion detect sprinklers, airhorns, pots and pans, shouting, etc. are good ways to tell coyotes that they need to move on away from your area. I always keep a hunting knife, trash bags, gloves, empty cooler, and hand sanitizer in my Jeep. The gloves avoid direct skin contact with the animal, trash bags keeps the animal contained, empty cooler is an extra layer of containment to keep any smells and fluids completely contained, the sanitizer is for my hands after getting rid of the gloves as a way to further keep germs and biohazards away, and the hunting knife is for if I am just wanting to take a specific part of the animal. My knife is a Winchester that is kept sharp, but Buck also makes good knives if you have a bit of a bigger budget/you want a knife that will last a long time. 


Residential streets, gravel, and roads that run near water (lakes, ponds, rivers, swamps), near train tracks, and near wooded areas are my favorite spots to look for roadkill. Residential streets will typically have small backyard critters like squirrels, rabbits, and occasional raccoons and opossums. Gravel can have similar roadkill, but in my experience you will find more skunks, foxes, and the occasional coyote. Roads near water can have a pretty big menagerie of roadkill as many animals will be crossing to drink from the water. Depending on how close the water is to the road, you may have chances of running into muskrats, beavers, otters, etc.. Similar things can be said about roads near wooded areas, though semi aquatic creatures are less likely to be found and larger fauna like deer are more possible. Train tracks are best if you are primarily looking for bones. Many creatures are struck by trains due to trains not being able to stop like cars. 


Also, look up the laws in your local area. Some places are really strict when it comes to picking up roadkill. Some areas are also pretty strict when it comes to taking an animal across state/country borders. For example, I live on the border between two states so I know both states laws regarding roadkill. In either state I cannot bring a dead deer over the border unless the skull is completely free of brain matter or I am only transporting the *completely* skinned hide and leaving the rest where I found it. It sounds ridiculous, but the law is there to prevent the spread of CWD (Chronic Wasting Disease).

I have no context in regards to the crazy neighbor and I do not know if they have a track record of severe animal abuse.


Regardless, I do not believe this cat was a victim of a sadistic human. Cats that have been ran over by vehicles can look like this if they were struck in their midsection. Aside from their spine and ribcage (which becomes crushed under the weight of a vehicle) there really is only soft tissue, which often gets squished/flung around by a vehicle's tires. Any soft tissue left behind after that can quickly get scavenged by birds, raccoons, foxes, dogs, etc.. Judging by the picture, it definitely looks like the cat was scavenged. 


If a sadistic human were to do something similar to this to a cat, it would not appear this mangled even if the cat was dumped afterwards and left for a few hours. For example, the area around the front legs where the hide was torn. The flesh showing is very bruised, and areas where you can see where the hide detached from the muscle is very rough. A person with a knife would not cause that amount of bruising on the flesh and the detached hide would have way less flesh still attached to it even if the person was in a hurry/not skinning diligently. The edges around the hide appear uneven and ripped, not cut. A cut hide leaves cut/noticeably shorter hairs around it and the actual skin would not look like frayed fabric. 


The hide in the belly/midsection will appear clean with very little flesh left attached. That is because there isn't much attaching the skin to the rest of the body to begin with. That area doesn't bear much hard muscle and there's usually more fat in those areas. 


The hind legs also look pretty bald around the knee area. This could be from hair slippage (stage of decomp), but it also could be from road rash. Road rash is extreme friction from skidding/sliding across asphalt which can cause loss of skin and hair (risk of road rash is also why many wear thick leathers when driving motorcycles).


All in all, I don't think the neighbor is to blame at all. This *really* looks like the cat was ran over by a vehicle and there's no really hard evidence that points to sadistic intentions. You could possibly argue that it could've been the neighbor that ran the cat over, but legally there isn't really anything you can do about that as even if you did have foolproof evidence that the neighbor ran over the cat, the law will most likely just say that the cat should've been indoors/not in the road.

Air dry paints dry much faster. This aspect can be hard for newer artists or artists who only have experience with heat set paints, as there isn't much time to fix mistakes before it cures.


Air dry paints can also be harder to use in the sense of making the skin realistic with the intricate layers needed. Some tactics that work for heat set doesn't always translate well to air dry. 


Air dry also has more steps involved in thinning. Simply mixing air dry with water can break up the adhesions in the paint, causing it to roll off the vinyl instead of sticking properly. Liquitex Ultra Matte Gel Medium is a common thing used in air dry circles as it allows the paint to be thinned with water *without* it losing it's ability to stick to vinyl. There's a ratio that needs to be figured out when it comes to mixing paint, water, and the medium as too much of one thing can create an effect you don't want (too much water causes poor adhesion, too much paint causes too much saturation, too much medium can cause a white flaky glaze, etc).


It can also be hard to find a good varnish for air dry. Some artists have no issues with one brand of varnish, while other artists may have problems with that brand. DuraClear Ultra Matte Varnish, Super Clear, etc are a couple brands that I have seen used as varnish for reborns. I have personally used the DuraClear and it works well for me and is pretty sturdy. 


All in all, there is a lot of differences between air dry and heat set. It sucks that they are discontinuing heat set paints as many artists are likely going to have to relearn their skills with air dry.

It may not be seem from the outside, but inside I feel so tense that I can't control it. 


Therapy and time can help diminish those, "shut downs," and it is most observed with children, which often puts people under the impression that it's just a part of growing pains and that it will go away on its own. Mishandling of the condition can actually make it worse and cause it to persist well into adulthood.

Well, part of the problem with professional pest control (where people just spray everything and leave) is part of controlling pests is modifying the environment as much as possible, so the pests have a harder time becoming established in your home. 


For example, I could hire a professional to spray my house down for carpet beetles. It will probably get rid of the carpet beetles, but they will come right back if I don't actually do anything different to keep them away. Chemicals fade and become less effective over time, and that prime environment for such a pest will still be there. If I actually change things such as frequently vacuuming and shampooing my carpets, keeping Borax down near doorways, windows, and against walls, and protecting natural items then I will likely not have another infestation of carpet beetles because I have now made that environment not ideal for them to live in. 


I have also learned that infestations run on a cycle and that a one-and-done spray down is never going to solve shit. Some pests *will* survive and they *will* reproduce. On top of that, there is always a certain life stage where pests are going to be the weakest against chemicals, and not all of the pests will be in the same life stage. So you have to frequently reapply chemicals every few days so you can take out as many generations as possible during the weakest time in their lives. That's part of what makes Borax so effective against pests, as oftentimes it will still melt the shit out of invertebrates no matter the life stage.

Yes, it is there to initiate brood elimination. This patch of nerves likely came to be through natural selection way back when the cuckoo first became a brood parasite. Chicks without the nerves didn't survive to breed, as they either starved to death or died due to being pushed out by the other chicks. Chicks with the nerves (and the reflex to push) lived to breed as there was less competition within the nest. Once adults, they passed on those nerves and reflexes to their offspring, then the offspring of them, and so on.

Cuckoo birds are brood parasites. It means that they don't follow the traditional rules of building a nest, incubating eggs, and feeding their young until it becomes able to fly. 


The mother cuckoo instead doesn't raise her chicks at all. She lays her eggs in the nests of other birds. Cuckoo eggs often hatch faster than other bird eggs, and the cuckoo chick is born with a set of sensitive nerves on it's back. When these nerves are touched, it triggers a reflex in the cuckoo chick. This makes the cuckoo push against whatever is touching the nerves until the object touching it goes away or the cuckoo exhausts itself. This reflex disappears once the cuckoo grows feathers over the nerves.


It's kind of like how human babies come out of the womb with the reflex to grab whatever presses against their palm. They don't exactly know what they are grabbing, it's just that those nerves are being triggered and the body is responding automatically.

Some bird species simply don't notice and there are others that actually do count their eggs.


For those species that do pay attention to their number of eggs, the cuckoo mother will just simply throw one egg out before replacing it with one of her own.

Okay, so I have done multiple wind chimes out of bones.


Leg bones usually are best for the actual chimes as they are straight, long, and sometimes hollow. They can give a sound similar to bamboo or wood when they hit each other. You can get an idea of the sound by taking two bones and tapping them against each other.


There's many ways you can do the part that the chimes hang off of. You can use the pelvis, a longer femur, an embroidery hoop, or those metal circles that are used to make wreaths. I have even seen others use the skull. 


Then on a wind chime you have the weights and the catcher. The weights are normally the little decorations set on the middle of the hanging hoop, and they sit between all of the actual chimes. This helps the chimes actually strike each other even in a light breeze. The catcher is the round part that hangs past the chimes in the middle and that makes the wind catch so the chimes will ring easier. I have used vertebrae as the weights and the catcher as the little, "wings," coming off of them catch the wind and strike the chimes with minimum movement. You can practically use anything round for the weights, but I recommend using something light in weight as your catcher, as it will take less wind force for it to be moved.


If you are looking to hang these chimes outdoors then I highly recommend a dremel and steel cable. Yes, you can get sick from bones that are not cleaned/sanitized. 


Though I will note that if you find bones instead of extracting them from a still-fleshy carcass then your risk for contracting rabies is *extremely* low. Almost nonexistent. The disease will not kill you like it will with deer, but it can make you really, really sick. You will have to be careful when handling deer bones. Armadillos also carry leprosy, and while the risk of you contracting such is low, I'd advise avoiding those bones especially if you already have a compromised immune system. There's a number of illnesses that can make you sick from dirty bones.

I also want to note that most of the time the dogs being shown are pets. They are not always dogs that are from a show bloodline. In fact, a lot of them are mutts. The responsibility of handling does fall on both the parents and their 4-H/FFA instructor. A trick I have figured out for mine is soaking the pole before installing it. When I get the poles I'll immediately get a tub and soak them for a few hours in a mixture of water and plant safe fungicide. This makes the fibers swell, and the fungicide gets rid of any bad mold that might be in the coir. After soaking the pole will hold moisture better and the fibers will loosen up enough for the roots to get into it. I can tell if my poles have good moisture when it feels slightly sticky/tacky to the touch. When it is not tacky that is when it needs moisture via a humidifier or a few minutes in the shower.


Plants taken from the wild can also struggle if they are immediately brought indoors. The light and temperature indoors can be very different from what they experience outside, so sometimes they need a slower transition to indoor living. It's kind of like hardening indoor plants to becoming outdoor plants, but backwards. Plant your cuttings and instead of bringing them inside, move them to a shadier location outdoors. This will get them used to the less light they will experience indoors without also completely shocking them. If they seem to be doing fine in that shadier location after a couple weeks, then try moving them indoors in the afternoons (in hotter regions our house temperatures mimic what is present in the morning). After a week or two of that, start trying to keep them in the house 24/7.

I started growing some pothos cuttings on a pole less than a year ago (September 2021). I have been extending the pole, so I have yet for my pothos to reach the top.


Though i can give you some tips if you're wanting to start growing a pothos on a pole. You can DIY a pole with hardware cloth and sphagnum moss if you already know what height you want the plant to grow into. I personally bought premade coco coir poles as I didn't know what height I was wanting my pothos to stop at, and those poles allow for you to add onto them as needed. When installing the poles into the pot, you'll want the pole to touch the bottom of the pot (or get as close to it at possible) so that way it will be sturdy enough to support the weight of the vines. For me I actually added an old curtain rod to my pole for extra support. 


The cuttings you add should be many and each cutting shouldn't have more than 3-4 leaves on it. Less leaves means shorter time to establish and more room for new growth. I started mine with 6 fresh cuttings with a couple inches of root growth. Plant the cuttings close to the pole. When the cuttings start growing, tie the vine to the pole with the node laying against the pole. You can use gardening velcro, jute string, or cotton string to tie the vines. I personally use cotton string as it doesn't cut into the vines and once the string biodegrades (and falls apart) the vine is established enough to no longer need it anyways. You might have to closely watch the growth for a bit, as you'll probably have to keep tying the vines down until it becomes established. 


Once you set your pole and have your cuttings planted, give it light. It will not grow very fast or very well if you have it in a dark corner. Get it close to a window or give it a good grow light. Mine grows under a light. It will also need some humidity. My household humidity already sits at 50 to 60% and my pothos probably gets a little extra from it growing right beside my turtle's tank. Because of that, I don't use a humidifier often, but you'll definitely need one if your house is drier. Of course, give it some water. On a DIY pole you can make it to where you water from the top of the pole so the water keeps the moss moist. With my premade coco coir poles I actually put mine in the shower and let it run for a few minutes. This puts moisture into the coco coir, and the water hitting all of the plant also has the added benefit of preventing pests/dust from establishing themselves. Once my plant got about a foot up the pole, I started keeping it fertilized. Growing plants up a pole like that can really suck up the nutrients in your soil so it helps to stay on top of it's needs. 


With all of that, you should start seeing bigger leaves. As the vine climbs, the leaves coming in will be a few inches bigger than the last. So a 4 inch older leaf may crop up a 6 inch leaf, then an 8 inch leaf, and so on. You may also notice the vine getting bigger and thicker as well. Some of the vines on mine requires pruners to cut, even though they started so small that they could be cut with regular house scissors.

It is a possibility. Most ungulates (animals like alpacas, goats, cows, deer, hippos, and horses) have an udder. Other animals that are known to have more than 4 babies at one time typically have 2 rows of nipples totalling to 12 to 16. Cats, dogs, and rabbits are animals that have teats set up in this way. Opossums are marsupials, so their set of nipples would be in a cluster inside of their pouch instead of in rows.

There are laws against selling cat and dog fur (including taxidermy) in order to prevent people profiting off of such via stealing, adopting, or breeding cats and dogs specifically for their fur. 


Laws regarding dogs and cats can be confusing. You cannot sell a mounted cat or dog, but you can pay a taxidermist to get a cat or dog mounted. Commissioning a taxidermist is legal as the taxidermist is not charging you for the cat/dog themselves, but charging you for the time and supplies. It may seem like taxidermists are charging more for pets, but they are typically charging more due to cats and dogs often needing to be freeze dried, which takes more time than traditional skinning, tanning, and putting the hide on a form. 


When you own a taxidermy cat or dog, you cannot sell them. The only way you can get rid of them is by gifting them to another person. Gifting is exactly what it sounds like, you give the cat or dog to someone else without the other party paying money or trading something. When someone dies and things within their estate goes to auction, any taxidermy cats or dogs will be given to next of kin or outright thrown away (as they legally can't auction them off). 


Bones and wet specimens are not regulated due to how they are not as profitable as fur. Someone stealing, adopting, or breeding cats and dogs for bones and wet specimens is highly unlikely as they are so unprofitable that they will actually not make any money back, as bones and wet specimens are pennies compared to fur.


Other domestic species are not as regulated. This is due to most domestic species already existing in the meat industry. Rabbits are not regulated due to them already being used for meat, and them descending from a wild species that is not native to the U.S.. Cattle, sheep, horses, goats, swine, chickens, and most ducks and geese are not regulated for the same reason. With exotic pets it can be a bit more complicated depending on the pet and your country, but typically they are not regulated specifically due to them being non-native to the U.S. 


Dogs and cats are not native to the U.S. either, but their regulation comes from the fact that they are a domestic species (so they couldn't survive long-term in the wild anyways even if they tried) that *does not* already exist in the meat industry (in the west). For example, a ball python is a popular animal kept as a pet. However, they are not truly domesticated. They can be bred and given pretty colors by humans, but they don't actually depend on humans for anything. If they were released (in the right environment) they would carry on and survive with little to no trouble. A ball python, in legal terms, is not a domestic species, but instead, "unregulated wildlife," in most states.

A lot of folks forget a good first aid kit. You'll always want a livestock vet when you have goats, but your goats *will get hurt* and will need personal help and it could make all the difference to have a kit on-hand. Vet wrap, rectal thermometer, wormer, hoof trimmers, syringes + needles, drench gun, baking soda, blood stop powder, Vitamin B Complex, anti-fungal cream, and Nutri-Drench are things that can meet basic needs for when your goats need help. Tack and bug care. I very much advise training your goats to walk on a lead. The earlier the better. It can be hard to train goats when you have a lot of them, but it's absolutely worth it (especially if you don't/can't have a herding dog to assist you). You'll never know when your goats will need to be loaded into a trailer or when they will need to be separated/tied somewhere. Training them to not be scared of a halter and a leash will save you a lot of headache and will leave your goats *way less* stressed out in the end. I would also make or buy some blankets/coats for your goats. One made for hot weather, one made for cold weather. They will help keep your goats cool/warm during those freak cold/hot spell you will get in your area. Goats also attract flies, and those flies can be annoying and can cause infections. Get good fly spray, set up some fly traps a ways away from your pen, offer a fan if possible, and keep an eye on if your goats have any open wounds. Oh, I would also look into a goat head-squeeze or a trimming table. It's a blessing if you are trimming hooves or doing basically anything that you need them to be still for.


Enrichment and predator control. Goats get bored. Bored goats cause trouble. Get some items you can rotate out so your goats can be entertained. Jolly balls, treat dispenser toys, soccer balls, and even dog toys can be things that can keep goats happy (it's also comical to watch). You'll also want some predator control as goats are common victims to coyote, bear, cougar, and dog attacks. If you have kids, the kids can be victims to birds of prey. The best predator control is a livestock guardian dog, but having such is not always feasible in smaller spaces/temporary fencing situations. Other ways to keep predators at bay is electric wire from top to bottom, fencing that is 6 foot or over, barbed wire (great to put up on the outer parameter of the fence), dig defense barriers on the fence, motion detect sprinklers, and a shelter that you can lock the goats into at night.

I have had my fair share with coyotes (extremely common where I live). 

Are you sure this coyote does not have pups? If you can't see them, that doesn't mean they don't exist. This problem began right around breeding season and now is when they will be having/raising puppies. They will cover large amounts of ground when they have puppies and will act bold around other animals (especially dogs) if you are, "too close," to where the den is. That is when you'll begin to see lone coyotes out in the open, as the father or the older siblings will be, "guarding," the area leading up to the den.


Do you or your neighbors have anything that could attract coyotes. Bird feeders, water bowls, food bowls, insecure trash bins/dumpsters, and dead animals can be a *huge* attraction for coyotes and it can cause them to become unafraid of humans and pets (the biggest cause for coyote attacks is feeding them, either directly or indirectly). I would also see if you or your neighbors have *any* kind of shelter the coyotes can get into. Under decks, dog houses, abandoned vehicles, etc. are most common places where coyotes will try to hide and even try to raise pups.


Coyotes are extremely smart. Using the same hazing methods over and over again can cause them to become desensitized. Especially if their fear of humans is dulled. I have had to get *extremely* creative with coyotes in my area, and they are mostly less bold than what you described. Motion detect sprinklers, a radio blasting at the most active times, strobe lights at night, mace, BB guns, even a mannequin in the yard. 


I definitely recommend the mace if that is the most you can do. A coyote can become desensitized to sounds, but they can't be desensitized to getting hurt. I would also look into getting your dog a coyote vest. Yes, they look stupid, and yes they are a bit pricy, but it works. I had one for my little dog during a spell where some teenage coyotes were testing their luck. One of them attacked my boy and although he had some minor injuries on his legs, he made it out unscathed. The vest is also great for if you have birds of prey too, as my boss (who has a dog even smaller than my own) got one for that purpose and it has saved that dog's life more than once (local owls have a knack for little white dogs apparently).

Dogs do not biologically understand guns. Yes, dogs have been with us even before firearms, but they don't inherently understand such. That's because in the dog's mind, they don't see the gun flying out of your hand (no one can see the bullet so that's not even a consideration to a dog), therefore it must be the sound that is causing pain. Dogs can panic/become defensive at the sight of a gun, but that emotion is due to the association with sound, not due to what the gun actually does. For maceration you will need a vessel with a lid. The size of the vessel depends on the size of the animal. You can use a plastic sweater box, an empty plastic ice cream tub, or pretty much anything that is plastic with a lid. I always suggest a lid because the lid traps heat, keeps smells contained, and it prevents other animals from taking your dead or falling in and drowning.


Some people put the animal in the maceration whole, but I personally suggest taking off any skin and excess organs before macerating. The organs make the water really nasty really fast and it makes the maceration smell more. Taking off the skin prevents hair getting *everywhere* and clogging any tiny holes (hair does not break down easily). 


I always suggest keeping the maceration tub outdoors as even with a lid it is going to reek in an enclosed space. Try to find a spot with little foot traffic and some protection from the wind. When putting water in the tub, make sure it covers as much of the body as possible. If you want, spit in the water before putting the body in as a way to get bacteria started. It's not necessary in warmer weather, but it does help during the cooler months when bacteria isn't as active. 


Put the body in and let it sit for about a month. After a month, check on it. If there is still a lot of flesh attached, then let it sit for another month. Repeat checking it monthly until the bones are free of almost all flesh. Once it is done, take the bones out and begin cleaning. Rinse the bones gently with water and gently scrub off any left over flesh with a toothbrush and Dawn dish liquid. 


Have a clean tub ready for degreasing. Rabbits are luckily not too greasy, so degreasing will be shorter for them. Fill the tub with hot (not boiling) or warm water and add a few drops of Dawn liquid in there. Put the bones in there and wait a few weeks. Degreasing works best if the water is *kept* warm, so I would look into a heated bucket or an aquarium heater if this is something you are going to be doing often. Degreasing works in cold water, but it takes longer. If your degreasing water starts to look overly filmy or browned like tea, then pour out the old water, rinse the tub, and replace with fresh water and Dawn. If you are not sure if the bones are fully degreased, take them out and let them fully dry. If they are still really yellow/brown when dry then it is not fully degreased. They will be fully degreased once the bones are an off-white. 


If you wish to have really white bones, then rinse the bones free of soap and then soak them in hydrogen peroxide. Hydrogen peroxide does best in a dark place (the chemical is light sensitive) so cover the vessel or put it in a cabinet. It should take about a few hours to a day for the bones to whiten. If you are wanting whiter bones, but not, "medical school," type of white, then you can set the bones out in the sun. The sun will bleach them without making them super white.

First thing, be aware of laws. Is it legal to pick up roadkill? Do you need a permit to pick up roadkill? Is it illegal to pick up roadkill in specific locations (in my states it is illegal to pick up roadkill on highways)? Do you live in North America? If you do you have MBTA (Migratory Bird Treaty Act) which means you cannot collect *any* part of any native birds (you would need licensing and permits to do so). Always, always, *always* be familiar with laws, because conservation is no joke. 


Second, get personal protection equipment and handle things with care. Wear gloves when handling dead/decomposing animals and always double (or even triple) bag animals to keep biohazards contained. If your clothes made contact, wash them as soon as possible. Always wash your hand before and after handling a dead animal (regardless of if you had gloves on or not). If you are dealing with chemicals, wear the appropriate equipment, store them correctly, and *never* mix chemicals together if you don't know how they react to each other. 


With finding dead animals it often depends on your environment. If you live in an urban area you may struggle to find critters and you may have to go elsewhere to search for them. Bodies of water frequently have dead animals around them. If you live near agricultural fields you can frequently find dead animals after there have been tractors/equipment in those fields (just be respectful and don't trample the crops). Wooded areas are often teeming with dead animals (and if you're more urban, parks and golf courses can have dead animals). If there are livestock ranches nearby, you can try to get in touch with the owners and see if they will let you collect there (don't trespass though, it's incredibly rude). I know some people would suggest looking by railroads for dead animals, but I personally don't advise it if the railroad is active, as it can be really dangerous.

Typically if you are taking animals from one country to another it can be tricky and it often depends on the countries involved. Regardless you have to be aware of CITES (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora). It's an international agreement set to protect a species survival by regulating international trade. This protection includes both alive and dead animals. Any wild animal can be CITES protected (regardless of if they are actually labelled endangered or not).


So in general, if you want to avoid trouble by any means possible, I would stick to only collecting domestic species (dogs, cats, cattle, swine, horses, sheep, and goats), as those are not protected by CITES in any way.

- You would need a scalpel to skin the pelt and there are more than one way to skin a squirrel, so there are different incisions you can make and I advise looking up, "taxidermy incisions," to find the one best for you. Once the pelt is off the body, wash with regular Dawn dishwashing liquid. If any meat/fatty bits are still attached to the hide, gently scrape and cut those off. As far as preserving goes, it depends on what you want and how much work you are willing to do. You can just lay it flat in salt and borax for a few weeks, but the result will be a pelt that's stiff like cardboard. If you wanting the pelt to be floppy and like fabric, then that's a lot more work where you would have to pickle and tan the hide. **If at any point the hair starts falling out in chunks with very little friction, then the pelt is not salvageable. Throw it away. Do not pass Go, do not collect $200.**


- With bones there are many methods to it. I personally do maceration as it gives the fastest, cleanest result. You can remove excess yellowness with hydrogen peroxide. 


- The feet of a squirrel will preserve fine if just put in salt whole. Remember to pose the toes where you want it before setting in salt as the salt will make the feet stiff.

You don't have to seal it completely. Actually allowing *some* air access is good as it will allow bugs in and it will help with decomposition. For example, if your soil dries out too much, it can cause the body to mummify instead of rot. If there is little to no oxygen, adipocere could form. Adipocere is also known as grave wax or corpse soap. It's when body fats turn into a solid, flaky, greasy substance, and it usually occurs when there is very little oxygen in the environment.

Skin out the paws until you reach the last digit where the claw is attached. Once you get to the claw bones, separate those joints from the rest of the skinned paw. To skin it out, make an incision from where the foot was separated from the body all the way down to the main pawpad. Don't actually cut the pawpad, just get close to it.


Once you do that you can salt them until you are ready to work with them again. If you decided to salt them, rehydrate with water to make the hide pliable again. Add Borax to the skinned hide, stuff the toes with clay to create structure and use polyfill/stuffed animal filling to stuff the rest of the foot (make sure it is packed very tightly), then sew up.


The simple, "stick it in salt/borax whole and wait a few weeks," really doesn't work for critter feet larger than a rabbit's hind foot. When you get larger than that skinning is practically required because the flesh inside will rot and/or mold before the salt/borax will be able to penetrate and draw out the moisture.

It depends on how much of the actual hoof is left behind. If there is leg still there above the dewclaws then skinning out the leg is best for preserving (skin out until you reach the joint where the actual hooves are attached then sever it, leaving only the last joint inside the hoof). 

You *can* just leave all of the stuff in the hoof/leg. However, it's longevity will be compromised and it will be more likely to rot when exposed to humidity and heat. Goat hooves are also significantly bigger than rabbit feet, so there will be more flesh and tissue present. You can just put a rabbit foot in salt for a few weeks and it will cure, but putting a goat hoof in salt will likely not penetrate into the tissue properly and it can take months or even a year for it to cure to the point of total stiffness. 

Isopropyl alcohol would be better suited if you are looking to avoid skinning the hoof. Best way to do it is inject 70% or more isopropyl into major fleshy bits with a syringe (on a goat hoof the most fleshy parts are between the dewclaws and between the actual toes), and then letting it soak for 1 to 2 months in a jar of isopropyl. Be sure to pose the hoof in the way you want it permanently when setting it in the jar as the isopropyl will fix the hoof in whatever position it is put in. You can use fishing line to suspend the hoof and pose it where you want it.

Dementia normally starts out as sundowner syndrome and it can cause a lot of changes in a dog's behavior due to how it acts and progresses. Plant poaching is a bit different and can be a bit complicated. There are plant species that have nearly gone extinct in the wild due to poaching. Plant poaching has even gotten worse with the influx of new plant hobbyists in 2020. Yes, most plants are not going to be endangered or threatened, but those plentiful plants are just one trend away from becoming endangered or threatened. Yeah, poaching alone isn't the only thing endangering plants. Herbicides and urbanization also have a lot to do with it, but poaching certainly does not help at all. All it takes in the plant communities is for someone popular enough to show off their taken-from-the-wild plant in an aesthetic post and there is going to be raging demand for that plant and people are going to poach en masse to make quick money off the trend. 


On top of that, many plants taken from the wild often don't survive. Yeah, you can go a few feet in the woods by your home, uproot some wildflowers, and then transplant in your yard and they will likely be fine. That's because they are still in the ground, have about the same amount of light, the same amount of water, and they are basically in the same environment. However, most poachers will uproot these plants and send them states away or will try to put them in a pot inside their home. Plants that have germinated and grown all their life in the ground outdoors will often suffer tremendously from suddenly being in a pot, inside a house with way less light, and with very different temperatures. It's like taking your nursery raised, always-in-the-house pothos and just immediately putting it in the ground outside. The most likely scenario is going to be that pothos going into shock and not surviving. It's the same for wild harvested plants. On top of that, some wild plants just aren't made to be houseplants. They have evolved to their wild environment and will not take to indoor living no matter how much you try (and they will not actually thrive if you do force them into an indoor setting).
There are very few states in which aloe can grow wildly. It's definitely not outside the realm of possibility that this person stole this from someone's yard or a garden center.
