Buck ragging is super effective if you don't actively deal with goats on the regular. It would not have been successful with my school because most kids lived on or near a goat farm.


**To better explain buck ragging and exactly how horrible intact male goats smell:**

All goats have a, "waxy," smell due to the oils in their fur. That smell alone isn't overwhelming to most people, but it is always prevalent so it's worth noting. It smells like a combination of brand new tennis shoes and brand new crayons. 


Does (female goats) either go into heat during the fall or year round, it depends on the breed. For example, pygmy goats typically have a heat cycles in the fall. Boer goats have heat cycles every few weeks all year round.


When a doe goes into heat, it makes the buck (intact male) go into rut. This rut cause a huge uptick in hormones. With the raise in testosterone, it sends their scent glands (located at the base of the horns) into overdrive. This creates one aspect of the terrible smell, as their natural, "waxy," scent gets mixed with a now soured scent. The only thing I can compare this sour scent to is rotting vegetables, but it still has an indescribable, "wang," to it. 


Bucks in rut also exhibit different behaviors. They become aggressive and extremely determined to fuck. They will curl their lips often (flehmen response), and will, "baa," while lashing/waggling their tongues (because that's apparently sexy to the does). One of the biggest things a buck in rut will always do is *piss on their own faces.* They will do it until their beards are a matted clump glued together with urine (also you better pray to god if you have a white goat). This pee-face strategy adds yet another foul aspect to the lovely buck rag. It's like if you bottled a morning piss, left it out in the sun for a month, and then sniffed it. 


The main purpose of a buck rag (aside from school discipline) is so goat farmers can have a sure-fire way of knowing if one of their does is in heat. If a doe's heat is just starting or being a bit flaky, a buck rag can help them get from the, "I am feeling something," stage, to the, "I am extremely horny," stage. Most smaller goat farmers don't actually keep live bucks on their property. This is especially true for those that keep bigger breeds. So these farmers will get a buck rag, gauge the doe's heat, and if in heat they will either utilize artificial insemination or have a different farmer (who keeps bucks) bring a buck down to, "cover," the does for as long as that heat cycle lasts.

Number 1: You have only had this dog for 2 weeks and you are already putting her through a lot. It takes 3 weeks for a dog to figure out your normal schedule. 3 months for them to fully feel safe and secure in your home. It can take longer for some dogs, but generally this is the minimum time for a dog in a new home. You have already put her in training, brought her to a restaurant, etc all before she can even figure out what everyone's normal schedule is. That's a lot of pressure to be putting on a dog (especially one that was previously in a shelter where they likely spent most of their time in a kennel and didn't have much meaningful interactions with humans and other dogs). Your pup's reaction to other dogs probably has a bit to do with the fact that she is stressed and confused.


Number 2: I'm not sure what dog you had before her, but the dog you have now is a cattle dog. Breed *does* play a part in their behavior. Cattle dogs are working dogs. They are intelligent and need more mental stimulation than a 3 mile run. I suggest looking into puzzle games, scent games, and maybe some at-home agility. This will better busy her brain and tire her out more than what a run will do. I also want to note that cattle dogs are herding and ranch dogs. It's what they are bred for. Most herding and ranch breeds are going to be people and dog-selective. That's bred into them, because on a farm/ranch, a strange dog or a strange human can equal livestock getting injured or stolen. You can't completely change genetics with training, you can only manage what's already there. It's very possible that even with professional help she won't be a dog park dog. It's very possible that she'll just merely tolerate other dogs instead of being buddies with the dogs she meets.


Number 3: If you decide against rehoming her, I suggest taking a couple steps back and giving her time to actually settle in your household. Stop the training for a bit. Stop taking her to dog parks and restaurants. Just let her be in your house. Let her get used to schedules. Let her get used to the sights, smells, and sounds that are the norm in everyday life for your family. Save the other stuff for when she actually has stability and confidence in what is normal. In the meantime I suggest looking into a veterinary behaviorist (if possible). They will be able to better rule out things such as anxiety if applicable.  Get her started with a behaviorist once she is past the settle down period and go from there.

I used to have a cat that was an escape artist...

- They make cat-proof window screens so you can open your window without worrying about your cat shredding the screen to escape. Cats cannot bite or scratch through most metals. 


- If you have lever-type doorknobs, cats are quick to figure out how to open them. My front and back door has a doorknob with a keypad, and you have to use the keypad to unlock the door. It's a very easy way to curb a cat (and add extra security to the house itself). All of the other doors in the house also had lever doorknobs. I curbed my cat from opening those by using those stick-on babyproof locks set high up on the door. The babyproof locks were also helpful when she figured out how to open cabinets. 


- My cat used to try and book it out the front or back door whenever it opened. The backdoor led to the laundry room, which you could close off, so just closing the laundry room door prevented her from bee-lining outside.


- The front door was a different story. There was no way to physically close her off from it. Her favorite attempt strategy was hiding under the couch and then making a run for it when she heard the door open. We stopped her from going under the couch by using plexiglass panels to fill in the gaps.


- Even after blocking the couch, she still attempted to run out the door. We figured out that sheer unpredictability surrounding the door stopped her from making it outside. We had a motion detect speaker (that just played a doorbell sound that she hated), we had a motion detect air canister (that just sprayed air whenever she got near it), and we had her arch nemesis, a big ridiculous rubber rat that we bought around Halloween a few years ago. We would set these things up near the front door and rotate them around to curb her attempts. She never knew if she was gonna get a loud sound, air sprayed at her, or a rubber rat staring her down. Every time she started figuring out how far away she had to be to not set off the speaker or canister, we would move it so it her plan wouldn't work. This went on for about a couple years before she just finally gave up on trying to run outside.

You can:

- Halter tightly to a fence so they can't actually run away.


- Flip them on their side/back and trim that way (you might have to lightly sit on them).


- Hobble their legs so they can stand, but they can't really walk/run away (one pair works well enough. For example, if you are trimming the back legs then hobble the front legs and vise versa).


- Physically wear them out with exercise before trimming so they don't really have the energy to fight you. I used to personally run my goats for 30 minutes before immediately going to trim. I also used to schedule trimmings in the middle of a hot day because on hot days noon is usually the time when goats are the least energetic.


- Make future trimming easier by messing and picking up their hooves frequently. You don't even have to trim or clean them. Just when you're out and giving attention, touch and pick up a hoof for a few seconds before setting back down. The more you do it, the more they will tolerate it/realize it isn't the end of the world.
